In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the thermal tolerance of aquatic ectotherms and its limits is affected by environmental factors and how these effects can be explained in the context of energy turnover.
the question of how organisms and ecosystems are affected by climate change and the role of oxygen and capacity-dependent thermal windows in this context.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the concept of oxygen- or capacity-dependent thermal limits is a promising tool for integrating climate change-related stressor effects on the ecosystem level.
oxygen supply to the tissues and the resulting thermal windows of aerobic performance characters form a primary link to the role and functioning of the organism at the ecosystem level.
the oxygen- and capacity-limitations of thermal tolerance are a matrix for integrating the effects of climate-related stressors in marine ecosystems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
climate change and its associated factors may affect species and ecosystems through the window of performance.
the oxygen supply to tissues is the primary link between the thermal window of aerobic performance and the window of aerobic scope, and that the latter determines the window of aerobic capacity.
the oxygen supply to the tissues and its resulting aerobic performance characters form a primary link of organismal fitness and functioning in the ecosystem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
climate-induced changes in the thermal window of performance and aerobic scope, and thus of aerobic capacity, are the key factors that link organismal fitness to the ecosystem level.
the oxygen- and capacity-limiting thermal window of performance is a key concept for understanding the effects of climate-related environmental changes on aquatic ecosystems.
